title: DDD: language, contexts, objects
idea: Domain-driven design (DDD) shapes code around the business: a shared language, bounded contexts where each term has one meaning, and entities and value objects inside them.

analogy.text: In a port, the harbour master's "ship" has a length and a berth. To customs, a "ship" is cargo and a flag.
analogy.breaks: In code, you write the translation between contexts yourself.

points: Ubiquitous language: class and method names match words the experts use.
A bounded context is a boundary where each model term has one meaning.
An entity has an identity that lasts while its attributes change.
A value object is defined by its values, is immutable, and compares by value.

steps.caption: The word 'customer' means something different in each context. Each context owns its own model.
In Sales, a customer is a buyer: name, basket and loyalty tier.
Sales does not call the others' classes. It publishes a fact other contexts can read.
Shipping translates the event into its own `Recipient`: an address and delivery slot.
Billing builds a `Payer` with a payment method. Same person, different model.
Each context can change its model alone. Only the event's shape is a shared contract.

code.title: A value object
code.caption: `Money` is frozen and compares by value. Add `fee.amount = 1; console.log(fee.amount);` and run: the write is ignored, and it still prints 500.

walk.text: `Object.freeze` makes the instance immutable: no field can be changed after construction.
`add` returns a new `Money` and refuses to mix currencies.
Equality compares the values, not the reference.
The original fee is unchanged; `===` still compares references.

code.title: An entity
code.caption: `Customer` is equal by `id`. A renamed customer is still the same customer.

pitfalls: Do not share one `Customer` class across contexts; each context models its own.
Never mutate a value object; return a new one from every operation.
Name classes in the experts' words, not `Manager`, `Data` or `Helper`.

quiz.why: `===` on objects compares references, so two separate objects differ. Value objects need an `equals` that compares fields.

takeaway: Speak the experts' language, draw context borders, then separate identity from value.

starters: How do I find the boundaries of a bounded context?
Should an address be an entity or a value object?
Is DDD worth it for a small LLD interview problem?
